title: Lakshmana's rage and restraint
hook: only the weak blame fate, Lakshmana says, and then he has to decide what to do with his strength
carry: the rage stays, he doesn't spend it

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana, loyal to the bone. Rama has done nothing wrong, he said, and I'll fight for him. Today, his argument, and his restraint.

A few days ago, Rama told Lakshmana not to blame Kaikeyi: what had happened was daiva, larger than any one person. It's a gentle idea, and Lakshmana hates it. He stands with his brow knotted, and Valmiki says he's breathing hard, like an angry snake in its hole. He answers with an argument people have quoted ever since, the other side of an old question: how much is fate, and how much is up to us?
screen: `DAIVA, RAMA SAID.` → `LAKSHMANA HATES IT.` → `HOW MUCH IS UP TO US?`

segments.voice: Here is Lakshmana's case. Fate is what weak people talk about. The brave don't sit waiting for it; a real hero pushes fate aside with his own effort. Call this fate, and you've given up before you've tried. Then he holds up his arms. These aren't for decoration. They're for protecting you. Today the people will see which is stronger, fate or me. Let me take the kingdom for you, and you rule it. It's a powerful speech, and Valmiki doesn't make it foolish. In Hindu thought, effort, purushakara, is honored as seriously as fate, and plenty of teachers would side with Lakshmana on another day. But watch Rama. He doesn't argue the philosophy again. He wipes away Lakshmana's tears and speaks to him as a brother. Know that I'm determined to keep our father's word. Stand with me in this. That's the whole answer. And Lakshmana listens, head lowered, still grieving, still angry, and silent. This is the restraint. He doesn't stop feeling the rage; he chooses not to spend it. He has the arms, the bow, the courage, and probably the soldiers. What he gives his brother is the hardest thing for a strong person to give: holding back. And at once the energy has somewhere to go. If you're going to the forest, Lakshmana says, then so am I.
screen: `ONLY THE WEAK TALK OF FATE.` · `THESE ARMS ARE FOR YOU.` · `RAMA WIPES AWAY HIS TEARS.` · `THE RAGE STAYS; HE DOESN'T SPEND IT.` · then, large: `THEN SO AM I.`

segments.voice: Close your hands into loose fists, and feel your own strength in them for a few breaths. Then slowly open them, palms up on your knees, and notice that the strength is still there. Breathe with them open; holding back isn't the same as being weak.
Purushakara, human effort, the old partner and rival of fate. Lakshmana argues that heroes push fate aside, then lowers his head, keeps his strength unspent, and chooses to go with Rama.
Your line: the rage stays, he doesn't spend it. Effort and restraint, in one brother. Day five hundred twenty-nine, done.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers often set Rama's speech on daiva, fate, beside Lakshmana's speech on purushakara, human effort, and leave listeners to weigh both.

original.note: Sanskrit puruṣakāra: human effort, what a person does; the old partner and rival of daiva, fate.

trapdoor: what you thought: Lakshmana gives up his anger.
what it means: he keeps the anger but chooses not to spend it, and turns it into following Rama.
what a scholar hears: Lakshmana's speech against fate is the counterweight to Rama's speech on daiva, and Valmiki lets both stand without declaring a winner.

chat.meaning: Rama didn't debate fate again. He wiped Lakshmana's tears and asked him to stand with him, and Lakshmana kept his strength unspent.
